text:
IN THE
SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Wang v. Epoch Press Ltd.,

2017 BCSC 136

Date: 20170130

Docket:
S153227

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Yu
Zhi Wang

Plaintiff

And

Epoch
Press Ltd., formerly known as Xin San Cai Enterprises Ltd.,

Frank Cui, Ying Lian Sun, Sue Zhang and Vanstar Printers Inc.

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Verhoeven

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for Plaintiff:

K.D.
Wiebe

Counsel for Defendants, Epoch Press Ltd.,
formerly known as Xin San Cai Enterprises Ltd., Frank Cui and Ying Lian Sun
and Vanstar Printers Inc.:

L.J.
Wihak

Counsel for Defendant Sue Zhang:

C.M.
Ansley

Place and Date of Trial/Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

December
6, 2016;

New
Westminster, B.C.

January
4, 2017

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

January
30, 2017

I.

Introduction

[
1
]

The defendants Epoch Press Ltd. (“Epoch”), Frank
Cui (“Cui”), Ying Lian Sun (“Sun”), and Vanstar Printers Inc. (“Vanstar”) apply
under the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
[
Rules
], R. 9-5 (1) (a), (b) and
(d) to strike out and dismiss all or parts of this action.  Alternatively the
applicants seek an order requiring the plaintiff to amend the Notice of Civil
Claim (“NOCC”) to disclose a cause of action within 30 days of the order.  The
application is supported by the remaining defendant, Sue Zhang (“Zhang”).

[
2
]

I will refer to Cui, Sun and Zhang as the
“personal defendants”.

[
3
]

The plaintiff acknowledges that some amendments
to the NOCC are necessary, and has presented a proposed Amended NOCC (the
“proposed ANOCC”).

[
4
]

The NOCC makes a number of claims that are
personal to the plaintiff, all arising out of her relationship with Epoch and
the personal defendants. The NOCC and the proposed ANOCC also set out claims
that are intended to form the basis of a derivative action on behalf of Epoch,
as against the personal defendants and Vanstar.  However, the plaintiff has not
obtained leave of the court to bring such claims under
s. 232
of the
Business
Corporations Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c. 57 [
BCA
], as is required.  The
applicants argue that in the absence of the required leave, the derivative
claims are clearly improper, without merit, and must be struck. The applicants argue
that the remainder of the NOCC should also be struck out, and the action
dismissed.

[
5
]

The plaintiff argues that the application should
be adjourned in order to allow her to obtain discovery.

II.

Legal Principles

[
6
]

Rule 9-5 of the
Rules
provides in part as
follows:

(1)        At any stage of a proceeding, the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b) it is unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d) it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may pronounce judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

(2)        No
evidence is admissible on an application under subrule (1) (a).

[
7
]

As mentioned, the applicants rely on subrules
(a), (b) and (d) above.

[
8
]

I adopt my comments in
Lessor v. Toll Estate
,

2015 BCSC 427
:

[14]         As noted, [the applicant]
applies pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a) and (d) for an order striking the pleadings
on the basis that they fail to disclose a reasonable cause of action, or,
alternatively, that they constitute an abuse of process. On an application
under Rule 9-5(1)(a), no evidence is admissible: Rule 9-5(2).

[15]         Pleadings must clearly define
the issues of fact and law. Rule 3-1(2) requires that a notice of civil claim
must:

(2)…

(a) set out a
concise statement of the material facts giving rise to the claim;

(b) set out the
relief sought by the plaintiff against each named defendant;

(c) set out a
concise summary of the legal basis for the relief sought;

…

[16]         I adopt my comments in
Stoneman
v. Denman Island Trust Committee
,
2010 BCSC 636
concerning the purpose of
pleadings:

16     The purpose
of pleadings is to clearly define the issues of fact and law to be determined
by the court. The issues must be defined for each cause of action relied upon
by the plaintiff:
Canadian Bar Assn. v. British Columbia
,
2008 BCCA 92

at paras.
59-60
, citing
Homalco Indian Band v. British Columbia
,
1998 CanLII 6658 (BC SC)
, [1998]
B.C.J. No. 2703 (S.C.); and
Keene v. British Columbia (Ministry of Children
and Family Development)
,
2003 BCSC 1544
.

17     In
Homalco
,
K. Smith J. stated at para. 5:

The ultimate
function of pleadings is to clearly define the issues of fact and law to be
determined by the court. The issues must be defined for each cause of action
relied upon by the plaintiff. That process is begun by the plaintiff stating,
for each cause, the material facts, that is, those facts necessary for the
purpose of formulating a complete cause of action.

[17]         Chief Justice McLachlin
emphasized in
R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.
,
2011 SCC 42
[
Imperial
]
that the plaintiff must clearly plead the facts upon which it relies in making
its claim:

[22] … A claimant
is not entitled to rely on the possibility that new facts may turn up as the
case progresses. The claimant may not be in a position to prove the facts
pleaded at the time of the motion. It may only hope to be able to prove them.
But
plead them it must
. The facts pleaded are the firm basis upon which the
possibility of success of the claim must be evaluated. If they are not pleaded,
the exercise cannot be properly conducted.

[emphasis added]

[18]         As observed by Justice Frankel
in
British Columbia (Director of Civil Forfeiture) v. Flynn
,
2013 BCCA
91
at para.
10
, the test for striking pleadings because they fail to disclose a
reasonable cause of action is well-known.  In
Imperial
, McLachlin C.J.C.
enunciated the test in these terms:

[17]      The
parties agree on the test applicable on a motion to strike for not disclosing a
reasonable cause of action under r. 19(24)(a) [now Rule 9-5(1)(a)] of the B.C.
Supreme Court Rules.  This Court has reiterated the test on many occasions.  A
claim will only be struck if it is plain and obvious, assuming the facts
pleaded to be true, that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action:

Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse
,
2003 SCC 69
, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 263, at para.

15
;
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, at p. 980.  Another
way of putting the test is that the claim has no reasonable prospect of
success.  Where a reasonable prospect of success exists, the matter should be
allowed to proceed to trial…

[19]         In
Cimaco International
Sales Inc. v. British Columbia
,
2010 BCCA 342
at para.
40
, Justice
Kirkpatrick provided the following guidelines for determining whether it is
“plain and obvious” that a claim will fail:

(1)  whether there
is a question fit to be tried regardless of complexity or novelty;

(2)  whether the
outcome of the claim at trial is beyond a reasonable doubt;

(3)  whether
serious questions of law or questions of general importance are raised or if
facts should be known before rights are decided;

(4)  whether the
pleadings might be amended; and

(5)  whether there
is an element of abuse of process.

[20]         A
successful application under Rule 9-5(1)(a) can lead to an order striking the
pleadings with leave to amend, or an order dismissing the claim outright. If
the defect in the pleading may be cured by amendment, the court may grant leave
to amend:
Henry v. British Columbia (Attorney General)
,
2012 BCSC 1401

at para.
38
. If, however, the claim is without legal foundation regardless of
how it is pleaded the court may dismiss the claim:
Henry

at para.
38
;
Extra
Gift Exchange Inc. v. Ernest & Twins Ventures (PP) Ltd
.,
2007 BCSC 426

at para.
22
.

[
9
]

The meaning of the terms used in subrules
19(24)(b) and (c) of the former
Supreme Court Rules
, B.C. Reg. 221/90,
now R. 9-5(1)(b) and (c) of the
Rules
, was discussed by Romilly J.
in
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (S.C.) at para.
47
:

Irrelevancy and
embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it is
difficult to understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco
Audio-Publishers Inc.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.). An
“embarrassing” and “scandalous” pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it
will involve the parties in useless expense and will prejudice the trial of the
action by involving them in a dispute apart from the issues:
Keddie v. Dumas
Hotels Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147 (B.C.C.A.). An allegation which
is scandalous will not be struck if it is relevant to the proceedings. It will
only be struck if irrelevant as well as scandalous:
College of Dental
Surgeons of B.C. v. Cleland
(1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66 W.W.R. 499 (B.C.C.A.). A pleading is
“unnecessary” or “vexatious” if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s
cause of action or does not advance any claim known in law:
Strauts v.
Harrigan
,
1992 CanLII 595 (BC SC)
, [1992] B.C.J. No. 86 (Q.L.) (B.C.S.C.). A pleading that is
superfluous will not be struck out if it is not necessarily unnecessary or
otherwise objectionable:
Lutz v. Canadian Puget Sound Lumber and Timber Co.
(1920),
28 B.C.R 39 (C.A.)
. A pleading is “frivolous” if it is obviously unsustainable,
not in the sense that it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because of the
doctrine of estoppel:
Chrisgian v. B.C. Rail Ltd. et al.,
[1992] B.C.J.
No. 1567
, (6 July 1992), Prince George Registry 20714 (B.C.S.C.).

[
10
]

The modern view is that novel claims should not
be struck at the pleadings stage:
Mohl v. University of British Columbia
,

2006 BCCA 70
at para.
40
, citing
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2
S.C.R. 959.

[
11
]

The “plain and obvious” test also applies to
applications under the other subrules of R. 9-5(1): see
Parmar v. Blenz
the Canadian Coffee Co.
,
2007 BCSC 1190
at para.
33
.

[
12
]

As to abuse of process, I adopt my comments in
Acumar
Consulting Engineers Ltd. v. The Association of Professional Engineers and
Geoscientists of British Columbia (APEGBC)
,
2014 BCSC 814
at paras.
28-30
:

[28]         Judges have an inherent and
residual discretion to prevent an abuse of the court's process:
Toronto
(City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63 (CanLII)
, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 77, at para.
35
.  There,
Arbour J. added:

35 …This concept
of abuse of process was described at common law as proceedings "unfair to
the point that they are contrary to the interest of justice" (
R. v.
Power
,
1994 CanLII 126 (SCC)
, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 601, at p. 616), and as "oppressive
treatment" (
R. v. Conway
,
1989 CanLII 66 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1659, at p. 1667).
McLachlin J. (as she then was) expressed it this way in
R. v. Scott
,

1990 CanLII 27 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 979, at p. 1007:

... abuse of
process may be established where: (1) the proceedings are oppressive or
vexatious; and, (2) violate the fundamental principles of justice underlying
the community's sense of fair play and decency. The concepts of oppressiveness
and vexatiousness underline the interest of the accused in a fair trial. But
the doctrine evokes as well the public interest in a fair and just trial
process and the proper administration of justice.

[29]         As can be seen from the
above-noted comments of McLachlin J., there is no bright line dividing
vexatious proceedings from those that are an abuse of the court’s process.  The
factors that signal a vexatious proceeding may also signal an abusive process.
However abuse of process is a wider concept which can capture any circumstance
in which the court's process is used for an improper purpose:
Freshway
Specialty Foods Inc. v. Map Produce LLC, et al
,
2005 BCSC 1485
at para.
52
.

[30]         The
categories of abuse of process are open.  Abuse of process may be found where
“the process of the court is not being fairly or honestly used, or is employed
for some ulterior or improper purpose; proceedings which are without foundation
or serve no useful purpose and multiple or successive proceedings which cause
or are likely to cause vexation or oppression”:
Babavic v. Babowech
,

[1993] B.C.J. No. 1802 (S.C.)
.

III.

Analysis

[
13
]

As noted, the plaintiff’s claims arise out of
her relationship with Epoch and the personal defendants.

[
14
]

Some of the basic facts asserted in the NOCC are
as follows:

a)

The plaintiff, the personal defendants and three other persons incorporated
or founded Epoch (as Xin San Cai Enterprises Ltd.) on June 2, 2004. These
individuals were appointed as the company’s directors and remain so (NOCC para.
1.28). (Or the personal defendants were
de facto
directors, (NOCC para. 3.22);
(the NOCC is ambiguous about this).

b)

Epoch was incorporated for these primary business purposes:

i.

as a commercial printing company;

ii.

to print a religious periodical called the
“Epoch Times”; and

iii.

to provide employment and profits for the founders
of the company.

c)

The plaintiff and the personal defendants are devout Falun Gong
practitioners.  Epoch was operated entirely by Falun Gong practitioners.

d)

The plaintiff contributed $180,000 (whether this is Canadian or US
funds is not clear) for shares in the company.

e)

The plaintiff was the company’s President and the managing director
of its business from 2005 until she was ousted on March 3, 2009.

f)

The plaintiff is owed salary of $224,900 by
Epoch.

g)

The plaintiff invested or loaned $267,000 USD to Epoch in 2005. Of
this $120,000 USD was provided by an anonymous investor.  The plaintiff was to
receive shares in Epoch for the loans or investments, but the shares were not
issued to her. Most of the money was not repaid.

h)

Beginning in 2008 the personal defendants conspired to terminate the
plaintiff’s control of the business of the company and to remove her as a
director.

i)

As Operations Manager, Cui, along with the other
personal defendants, failed to collect receivables owed to the company in the
amount of $400,000, resulting in the need for the company to issue shares to
Sun, thus diluting the shareholdings of the plaintiff.

j)

The personal defendants caused a lawsuit to be
brought against Epoch by a newspaper, the Asian Pacific Post, which Epoch was
under contract to print.

k)

The personal defendants misappropriated $18,000 from Epoch.

l)

On March 3, 2009 the personal defendants
prepared a forged shareholders’ resolution purporting to remove her as a
director, and terminated her employment and position as President with Epoch.

m)

In 2009 the personal defendants and Epoch agreed to pay the
plaintiff unpaid accumulated salary as well as repay her shareholder loans.
These contractual obligations were breached.

n)

The personal defendants have refused to provide audited financial
statements for Epoch, or financial reporting or information.

o)

The personal defendants transferred Epoch’s assets and its business to
Vanstar, rendering Epoch insolvent.

p)

Sun is the sole director of Vanstar.

q)

Cui, Zhang and Sun defamed the plaintiff in 2007 – 2009 by making
various defamatory comments about the plaintiff (the plaintiff proposes to abandon
the defamation claims).

[
15
]

The plaintiff makes numerous claims, expressed
in terms of numerous legal causes of action. These include, non-exhaustively:
conspiracy to cause economic harm;  intentional interference with economic and
contractual interests; deceit; fraud; negligence; misrepresentation; knowing
assistance in breach of fiduciary duty; knowing receipt; breach of fiduciary
duty by the personal defendants to the plaintiff, and to Epoch; breaches of
contracts; breach of employment obligations by Cui; and numerous derivative
claims on behalf of Epoch. The NOCC also seeks orders for financial audits; the
rectification of Epoch’s corporate records; and injunctive relief against
Vanstar.

[
16
]

The proposed ANOCC abandons the defamation
claims but adds claims for relief against oppression under
s. 227(3)
of the
BCA
,
and claims for breach of fiduciary duty against the personal defendants based
upon their relationship with the plaintiff as Falun Gong co-religionists.

[
17
]

The plaintiff acknowledges that she brings her
claims in four distinct legal capacities: as an employee of Epoch; as a
director of Epoch; as a shareholder; and as a creditor.

[
18
]

On the basis of the pleadings, the personal
defendants also occupied several distinct legal roles: as individuals; as directors,
or perhaps
de facto
directors; as shareholders; as officers or employees
of the company (i.e. in the case of Cui); as contracting parties with the
plaintiff, or perhaps as guarantors or indemnitors of Epoch’s obligations; and
as co-religionists.

[
19
]

The fundamental difficulty with the NOCC is that
it fails to make clear what claims are being made against which defendants, and
in which capacity each defendant is alleged to be liable. The NOCC is also often
unclear as to the capacity in which the plaintiff is advancing the claims, or
seeking to do so. Similarly it is often unclear as to what facts are relied on
in relation to the myriad causes of action and remedies sought.

[
20
]

The proposed ANOCC adds further claims and is
not a significant improvement in terms of clarity.

[
21
]

Generally, the NOCC and the proposed ANOCC are
unclear as to whether the plaintiff is seeking to advance claims on her own
behalf or on behalf of the company.

[
22
]

For example, in relation to the allegations of “conspiracy
to cause harm to the plaintiff” in paras. 58-59 of Part 1 of the NOCC, the
plaintiff blends allegations that seem to relate to personal loss to her, such
as matters relating to her termination as President and a director and the
company’s failure to issue shares to her, and allegations that seem to relate
to loss to Epoch, such as allegations that the personal defendants advised Epoch’s
staff that the company was insolvent and encouraged the staff to strike. These
allegations are lumped together in the NOCC and collectively defined as the
“Harmful Acts”. The Harmful Acts and several other groups of allegations
(defined as “Misrepresentation”, “[Asian Pacific Post] Incident”, “Fraudulent
Termination”, “Failed Dissolution” and “Unlawful Conversion”) are alleged to
form the bases of personal claims on behalf of the plaintiff in some capacity
against the personal defendants in some capacity, but also to form the basis
for the intended derivative action on behalf of Epoch.

[
23
]

Another fundamental difficulty is that the plaintiff
wishes to bring proceedings on behalf of the company as a derivative action,
but has not sought and obtained leave of the court for that purpose.  This is
not a case where the plaintiff is seeking to advance personal claims for
oppression, which might potentially in some circumstances also be grounds for
derivative claims. Here, the plaintiff wishes to assert both types of claims,
but has not distinguished them. If the claims are fundamentally derivative in
nature, in that they are for loss to the company and do not form the basis for
personal claims by the plaintiff, then unless leave is granted, they should be
struck:
Hoet v. Vogel
,
[1995] B.C.J. No. 621 at para. 21
;
Robak
Industries Ltd. v. Gardner
,
2007 BCCA 61
; aff’g
2006 BCSC 1538
[
Robak
].

[
24
]

It is unknown what if any claims the plaintiff might
be granted leave to advance on behalf of Epoch.  It is unknown what personal
claims might remain if leave is not granted. As noted there is much overlap or
potential for overlap between her personal claims and the claims she seeks to
advance on behalf of the company.

[
25
]

Another difficulty is that on the basis of the
NOCC as filed and the proposed ANOCC, the plaintiff is suing Epoch at the same
time as she is proposing to bring claims on its behalf. This may be a factor
for the court to consider if an application is made for leave to commence a
derivative action.

[
26
]

The applicants contend that several of the apparent
claims are without merit. For example, they argue that pursuant to the rule in
Foss
v. Harbottle

(1843), 67 E.R. 189 (Ch.) [
Foss v. Harbottle
]
, a director
or shareholder of a corporation does not have a personal cause of action for
loss of investment or share value based on a wrong done to the corporation. The
applicants rely on
Hercules Management Ltd. v. Ernst & Young
,
1997 CanLII 345 (SCC)
, [1997]
2 S.C.R. 165 and
R.L.T.V. Investments Inc. v. Saskatchewan
Telecommunications
,
2009

SKCA 83
for this proposition.  They argue
that to the extent that the plaintiff is seeking to advance such claims, they
are without merit.  They argue, relying on
Robak

at para.
38
, that in
order to establish a personal claim for loss of her investment as a
shareholder, the plaintiff must have both an independent relationship with the
wrongdoer, and a loss that is independent to that of the company to which the
wrong has been done.

[
27
]

The applicants point out that there is a
distinction between claims that are alleged to be derivative, and claims based
upon oppression, citing
1043325 Ontario Ltd. v. CSA Building Sciences
Western Ltd.
,
2016 BCCA 258
[
CSA Building Sciences
] at paras.
48
,
54, 71-78. To the extent the plaintiff wishes to advance claims for oppression,
the applicants argue that she must “show particular prejudice or damage beyond
the diminution in value of his or her shares as a result of the allegedly
oppressive conduct” as set out at para. 78 of
CSA Building Sciences
.

[
28
]

The applicants also argue that Canadian law is
clear that directors do not owe fiduciary duties to their fellow directors.  Rather,
directors owe a duty of care and fiduciary duty to act in the best interests of
the company; here the applicants rely on
Peoples Department Stores Inc.
(Trustee of) v. Wise
,
2004 SCC 68
.  Furthermore, the applicants submit that
the actions of the directors of the company are the actions of the company; a
company can only act through its directors.

[
29
]

Finally, the applicants argue that if the
plaintiff now wishes to add claims of breach of fiduciary duty based upon the
personal defendants being Falun Gong co-religionists, then that claim is also
without merit because the proposed pleading does not disclose a recognized
category of fiduciary duty or plead any of the elements necessary to establish
a new category, and because there is no
prima facie
case that any of the
elements exist. They rely on
Frame v. Smith
,
1987 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 99 and
Lac
Minerals Ltd. v. International Corona Resources Ltd.
,
1989 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 574.
In this respect a difficulty on this application is that the proposed ANOCC has
not been filed and, as a result of my judgment on this application, a different
pleading will be required. It is premature to assess the viability of this
apparently novel cause of action.

[
30
]

The plaintiff argues that her claims are
complex, legally and factually, because the material events took place over
several years, because she advances her claims under a number of causes of
action and in various capacities, and because the defendants also occupied
varying roles.  Therefore, if I understand the argument correctly, the
plaintiff argues that the court should allow her latitude in relation to her
pleadings at this stage. The plaintiff suggests that the pleadings can be
amended and refined over the course of the proceedings.

[
31
]

However without clarity as to what causes of action
the plaintiff alleges, in what capacity, and against which party in what
capacity, and on what facts, the court cannot properly assess the viability of
the plaintiff’s claims. The defendants are unable to understand the case they
must meet.

[
32
]

The NOCC and the proposed ANOCC fail to fulfill
the basic purposes of pleadings, that is, to clearly define the issues of fact
and law to be determined by the court. The plaintiff’s pleadings fail to set
out the material facts relating to the various, and numerous, causes of action
referred to.

[
33
]

Justice Voith’s comments in
Canfor Pulp
Limited Partnership v. Siemens Building Technologies Ltd.
,
2016 BCSC 2089

are applicable:

[22]
When several causes of action are being alleged against multiple parties, a
statement of claim or third party notice must clearly identify what facts
relate to what cause of action and to which party.  It is inappropriate to
lump defendants together in a pleading and to make blanket allegations against
them, unless those defendants were in an identical relationship with the
plaintiff.  Such pleadings are necessarily imprecise, are overly general,
and make it impossible to discern on what basis each of the defendants could be
held liable.  Such a pleading may be struck for failing to clearly define
the issues of fact and law that are to be determined by the court and/or for
being vexatious, prejudicial to a fair trial of the proceeding, and an abuse of
process; see
Stoneman v. Denman Island Local Trust Committee
,
2010 BCSC
636
at para.
27
;
The Campbell River Indian Band C.A.
at
paras. 76-77;
Forde v. Interior Health Authority
,
2007 BCSC 1706
at
paras.
17-18
; and
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2013 BCSC 1143
at paras.
53-54
.

[
34
]

Rather than focusing her claims, the plaintiff
has chosen to attempt to pursue a plethora of causes of action against numerous
defendants in varying capacities based upon many factual allegations stretching
over several years. The difficulties inherent in properly pleading such claims
are self-made.  No matter how complex the facts and causes of action the
plaintiff wishes to assert may be, she is not relieved of the responsibility of
properly pleading them. Indeed, the approach taken by the plaintiff only serves
to emphasize the need for intelligible, coherent pleadings.

[
35
]

The plaintiff also argues that, “[i]f the
pleadings cast too wide a net at this stage, are unclear or assert causes of
action which ought properly to be brought by the Company it is the direct
result of the Plaintiff being illegally removed and blocked from access to all
information and thus having to use third parties and publicly available records
to determine what happened to her own company.”

[
36
]

As noted, the plaintiff argues that based upon
the foregoing the action should not be struck at this stage, but instead the
application should be adjourned to permit her to obtain discovery.

[
37
]

As stated by McLachlin C.J.C. in
R. v. Imperial
Tobacco Canada Ltd.
,
2011 SCC 42
[
Imperial Tobacco
], the plaintiff
must plead the facts upon which its claim relies, whether or not the plaintiff
is in a position to prove those facts.

[
38
]

It is axiomatic that the pleadings define the
issues before the court. Thus, they define the scope of discovery, since the
issues determine what information must be disclosed through discovery. The
issues also determine what evidence is relevant at trial. It is illogical to
suggest that discovery processes should proceed without adequate pleadings: see

SunOil Ltd. v. Big Snowy Resources L.P.
,
2015 BCSC 167
at para.
19
,
citing
Imperial
Tobacco
at para.
22
.

[
39
]

It seems that the NOCC sets out facts which
could potentially form the basis of viable causes of action. Thus, dismissal of
the claim in its entirety is not appropriate, at this juncture.

[
40
]

Where a pleading is so prolix and confusing that
the other party cannot understand the case to meet, it should be struck out
pursuant to R. 9-5:
Gateway Building Management Ltd. v. Randhawa
,
2013
BCSC 350
at para.
18
, citing
The Owners, Strata Plan LMS3259 v. Sze Hang
Holding Inc.
,
2009 BCSC 473
at para.
36
.  Also, as noted, the court is
unable to determine whether any of the causes of action asserted should be
struck.

[
41
]

To the extent the plaintiff seeks to advance
derivative claims, she must seek leave of the court. Thus the derivative claims
she makes in the NOCC must be struck out.  The difficulty is that the pleadings
are anything but clear as to what claims are in reality derivative and which are
not.

[
42
]

Assuming the plaintiff wishes to pursue a
derivative action, in my view the starting point must be for her to bring an
application for leave to do so. Plaintiff’s counsel advised me that it was her
intention to do so.  If the plaintiff wishes to continue to pursue personal
claims, she must do so in an amended NOCC that fulfills the purposes of
pleadings and does not assert derivative claims.

[
43
]

In my view the appropriate remedy in this case
is similar to the remedy that I ordered in
Stoneman v. Denman Island Local
Trust Committee
,
2010 BCSC 636
.  I order as follows:

a)

The NOCC is struck out in its entirety;

b)

The plaintiff has leave to amend the NOCC to
properly plead causes of action that are not derivative in nature;

c)

The amended NOCC must be filed within 90 days;

d)

The action is stayed in the meantime;

e)

If the plaintiff fails to file an amended NOCC
within 90 days, the defendants are at liberty to bring an application to have
the claim dismissed; and

f)

The defendants will be at liberty to apply to
strike out and dismiss all or any part of the amended pleading on any ground
available.

[
44
]

The applicants have been substantially
successful. They are awarded costs of the application, payable in any event of
the cause.

“The Honourable Mr. Justice Verhoeven”
